units.title: Unit 67 — Opinions, agreeing and disagreeing
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 140–141 (PDF pages 141–142).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Ask for opinions about specific people or things and about general topics.
Introduce personal opinions with personally, in my opinion, my view and my feeling.
Report the views of other people or news sources with say and according to.
Express complete or partial agreement and politely introduce a contrasting view.
Use strong agreement and disagreement accurately and avoid common agreement errors.

items.word: What do you think of it?
items.example: What do you think of my new glasses?
items.note: Use think of when asking someone to evaluate a particular person or thing.

items.word: What do you think about it?
items.pt: O que você pensa sobre isso?
items.example: What do you think about the plans for the town centre?
items.note: Use think about to ask for a view on a general subject or issue.

items.word: How do you feel about it?
items.pt: Como você se sente em relação a isso?; o que acha disso?
items.example: How do you feel about working at weekends?
items.note: How do you feel about + noun or -ing asks for an attitude or opinion.

items.example: Personally, I think the new timetable is better.
items.note: A natural way to introduce your own view; follow it with a clause.

items.example: Personally, I feel we should discuss the risks first.
items.note: The word feel can introduce an opinion, not only an emotion.

items.example: In my opinion, the museum should stay open later.
items.note: Say in my opinion, not on my opinion or in my meaning.

items.pt: minha opinião é; meu ponto de vista é
items.example: My view is that the team needs another engineer.
items.note: My view is that + clause expresses a personal position.

items.pt: minha impressão é; minha opinião é
items.example: My feeling is that we should give everyone more time.
items.note: Often used for a judgment or opinion rather than a physical feeling.

items.word: I don't think it's a good idea.
items.pt: não acho que seja uma boa ideia
items.ipa: /aɪ dəʊnt θɪŋk ɪts ə ɡʊd aɪˈdɪə/
items.example: I don't think it's a good idea to leave without a map.
items.note: Negative opinions often sound more natural with don't think + a positive clause.

items.pt: o jornal afirma; segundo o jornal
items.example: The newspaper says the station may close next year.
items.note: Use the newspaper says (that) to report what was published, not it is written in the newspaper.

items.pt: segundo o jornal; de acordo com o jornal
items.example: According to the paper, the project has been postponed.
items.note: Attributes information to a source without necessarily endorsing it.

items.example: According to the newspaper, the library will reopen in June.
items.note: An alternative to the newspaper says; introduced in the practice activities.

items.example: I agree with you. The instructions need to be clearer.
items.note: Say I agree with you, not I am agree with you.

items.example: Do you agree that we should start earlier?
items.note: Agree is a verb: use do in a present-simple question, not are you agree.

items.example: I totally agree that safety should come first.
items.note: Totally indicates complete agreement; a strong affirmative response.

items.example: I partly agree, but the plan will be expensive.
items.note: Partly means you agree with some, not all, of an opinion.

items.word: I agree to a certain extent.
items.example: I agree to a certain extent, although we still need more evidence.
items.note: A measured response expressing partial agreement.

items.pt: concordo até certo ponto; concordo em parte
items.example: I agree to some extent, but we cannot ignore the costs.
items.note: A shorter alternative to to a certain extent.

items.example: That's true, but we also need to consider the budget.
items.note: A polite way to acknowledge a point before introducing disagreement.

items.pt: entendo o que você quer dizer
items.example: I see what you mean, but I prefer the simpler design.
items.note: Indicates understanding; it does not necessarily mean full agreement.

items.word: I think that's a good point.
items.pt: acho que esse é um bom argumento; acho válida essa observação
items.example: I think that's a good point, although we need to check the figures.
items.note: Point means a useful idea or argument in a discussion.

items.pt: entendo seu ponto de vista; reconheço seu argumento
items.example: I take your point, but the proposed date is too soon.
items.note: Often signals that you understand or partly accept a point before disagreeing.

items.word: I see what you mean, but
items.pt: entendo o que você quer dizer, mas
items.example: I see what you mean, but I think we should ask the client first.
items.note: A common, polite structure for partially disagreeing.

items.word: I agree to some extent, but
items.example: I agree to some extent, but there are still important differences.
items.note: Concedes part of the argument before giving a different opinion.

items.pt: esse é um bom argumento, mas
items.example: That's a good point, but we may not have enough staff.
items.note: Introduces disagreement without dismissing the other person.

items.example: I take your point, but a later meeting might be easier for everyone.
items.note: A respectful form of partial agreement followed by an objection.

items.word: I feel very strongly about this.
items.pt: tenho uma opinião muito firme sobre isso; isso é muito importante para mim
items.example: I feel very strongly about protecting the local woodland.
items.note: Feel strongly about + noun or -ing expresses a deeply held view.

items.pt: você tem toda a razão; você está absolutamente certo
items.example: You're absolutely right. We must test the equipment before use.
items.note: Absolute agreement; right refers to a correct view or judgment.

items.example: You're absolutely wrong about the opening times; the shop closes at six.
items.note: Very direct, strong disagreement; may sound confrontational.

items.pt: não concordo nem um pouco; discordo totalmente
items.example: I don't agree at all with that explanation.
items.note: At all strengthens the negative; a firm disagreement.

items.example: I completely disagree that closing the park would make it safer.
items.note: Completely makes the disagreement absolute.

items.example: I disagree completely with that recommendation.
items.note: Alternative word order with the same strong meaning.

items.pt: não sei se concordo; não tenho certeza de que concordo
items.example: I'm not sure I agree with your conclusion.
items.note: A less direct way to express doubt or disagreement.

items.example: I disagree with you about the best way to organise the work.
items.note: Disagree with a person; disagree about an issue.

sectionsChecked: A: Asking someone for their opinion
B: Introducing your own opinion and common mistakes
C: Giving the opinion of others
D: Agreeing and disagreeing with someone and common mistakes

units.title: Unit 68 — Likes, dislikes, attitudes and preferences
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 142–143 (PDF pages 143–144).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Functional language: likes, attitudes and choices
learningObjectives: Express a range of enthusiasm and dislike, from love and be into to cannot stand.
Agree or disagree with positive and negative statements using so, neither, me too and me neither.
Talk about attitudes, interests, former habits and similarities between people.
Distinguish used to + base verb from get used to + noun or -ing.
Compare choices using prefer A to B, would prefer to and would rather + base verb.

items.example: I love the way this room looks in the morning.
items.note: Love expresses strong positive feelings; it can take a noun or an -ing form.

items.pt: gosto muito disso; sou muito fã disso
items.example: I'm really into jazz at the moment.
items.note: Informal: be into + noun or -ing means be very interested in or enthusiastic about.

items.word: I like a lot of pop music.
items.ipa: /aɪ laɪk ə lɒt əv pɒp ˈmjuːzɪk/
items.example: I like a lot of the songs on that album.
items.note: A lot of modifies the number of songs or types of music liked; compare I like pop music a lot, where a lot describes intensity.

items.pt: eu até gosto disso; gosto razoavelmente disso
items.example: I quite like the restaurant, although it is a little noisy.
items.note: In this context quite like often expresses moderate rather than very strong enthusiasm.

items.pt: não me importo com isso; para mim está bom
items.example: I don't mind the music if you keep it quiet.
items.note: Expresses acceptance or neutral feeling; often means it is OK.

items.word: I'm not very keen on it.
items.pt: não gosto muito disso; não sou muito fã disso
items.example: I'm not very keen on horror films.
items.note: Be keen on + noun or -ing; not very keen is a mild, polite negative opinion.

items.example: I can't stand the noise from the building work.
items.note: Informal, strong dislike; cannot stand can take a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: I hate waiting in long queues.
items.note: Hate expresses strong dislike; followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: I dislike driving when the roads are icy.
items.note: More neutral/formal than hate; can take a noun or -ing.

items.pt: eu também; eu também gosto ou faço isso
items.example: I love this café. So do I!
items.note: Agree with a positive present-simple statement such as I like or I love.

items.pt: eu também sou; eu também estou
items.example: I'm really interested in space. So am I.
items.note: Agree with a positive statement using am, such as I am interested.

items.example: I've got a bicycle. So have I.
items.note: Agree with a positive statement using have, including have got.

items.example: I enjoy walking by the sea. Me too!
items.note: An informal positive agreement response across several structures.

items.pt: eu também não sou; eu também não estou
items.example: I'm not keen on that proposal. Neither am I.
items.note: Agree with a negative statement using am.

items.pt: eu também não consigo; eu também não posso
items.example: I can't concentrate with loud music. Neither can I.
items.note: Agree with a negative statement using can.

items.example: I don't enjoy scary films. Neither do I.
items.note: Agree with a negative present-simple statement using do.

items.example: I don't like that band. Me neither.
items.note: Informal response agreeing with a negative statement.

items.example: I love that song. Really? I don’t.
items.note: Expresses a contrasting opinion after a positive present-simple statement.

items.example: I'm really into running. Really? I'm not.
items.note: Responds negatively to a positive statement with be.

items.example: I don't mind waiting for a few more minutes.
items.note: Mind is normally followed by an -ing verb when naming an activity.

items.word: I can't stand getting up early.
items.example: I can't stand getting up early in winter.
items.note: Cannot stand + -ing communicates a strong dislike of an activity.

items.pt: atitude em relação a; postura diante de
items.example: His attitude to teamwork has changed over time.
items.note: Attitude to + noun refers to how someone thinks or feels about a subject.

items.pt: costumava; fazia no passado, mas não necessariamente agora
items.example: I used to play tennis every Friday, but now I go swimming.
items.note: Past habit or state: used to + base verb. Different from be/get used to + noun or -ing.

items.example: Computer games don't interest me as much as they once did.
items.note: Interest is a verb here; does not interest me means I do not find it interesting.

items.pt: tenho interesse nisso; isso me interessa
items.example: I'm interested in learning another language.
items.note: Be interested in + noun or -ing. Not I am interest in.

items.pt: interesses; atividades de que se gosta
items.example: The children have very different interests.
items.note: Plural noun for subjects or activities someone enjoys.

items.example: My brother and I have the same interests in music.
items.note: Describes overlapping preferences and activities.

items.example: They work together but have nothing in common outside work.
items.note: No shared interests or similarities; opposite: have a lot in common.

items.example: We have a lot in common, including our love of cycling.
items.note: Share many interests or characteristics.

items.pt: nem um pouco; de forma alguma
items.example: I don't enjoy crowded places at all.
items.note: Strengthens a negative sentence; here not at all is not a reply to thanks.

items.example: It takes time to get used to working in a new office.
items.note: Get used to + noun or -ing means become familiar with; to is a preposition.

items.example: She is used to working on her own.
items.note: Be used to + noun or -ing describes a familiar situation, not a past habit.

items.example: I've got used to the noise from the busy street.
items.note: The present perfect suggests an adjustment has already happened.

items.example: I'm getting used to using the new software.
items.note: Describes the ongoing process of becoming comfortable with something.

items.example: I prefer walking to driving for short journeys.
items.note: General preference: prefer A to B, not prefer A than B.

items.example: Which do you prefer, tea or coffee?
items.note: Asks about a general preference or choice.

items.example: Which would you prefer for tonight, a concert or a film?
items.note: Would makes the question about a particular or hypothetical choice.

items.example: I'd prefer to stay at home this evening.
items.note: Would prefer + to-infinitive expresses a preference on a particular occasion.

items.example: I'd rather stay here than go out in the rain.
items.note: Would rather + base verb (without to); an alternative to would prefer to.

items.example: I'd rather go home now and finish the work tomorrow.
items.note: An exercise-tested reformulation of I would prefer to go home.

items.example: I like this neighbourhood very much.
items.note: In an affirmative sentence with like, include the object: I like it very much.

sectionsChecked: A: Likes and dislikes, agreement/disagreement responses and language help
B: Attitudes and interests, common mistakes and getting used to things
